writing.exampleCaption: Tests live beside the code and can see its private parts.
writing.explanation:
`#[test]` registers functions with the test harness. A `#[cfg(test)]` module is excluded from ordinary builds, including `cargo build --release`, but included by `cargo test --release`. Test mode and optimization profile are separate choices. Unit tests sit beside the code and can reach its private details; integration tests live in `tests/` and see only the public API, which is a useful check on your own interface.

A test records an observable promise. `#[test]` marks a function that the test harness runs under `cargo test`; an assertion compares the actual value with a prediction. The sample puts tests beside the implementation in a `#[cfg(test)]` module, which is a good place for small unit tests of edge cases and private helpers. The module is only compiled when testing, so it does not become a normal production code path.

Start with a function that adds two numbers. Test a typical case, zero, and a boundary that might reveal overflow or an incorrect sign. Name tests for the behavior they protect rather than the implementation line they execute. If a test fails, its assertion should tell you what input produced the mismatch. A test that merely repeats the function's code is weak: it can share the same mistake. Prefer a simple expected result you can justify independently.

Integration tests under `tests/` compile as separate crates and call the public library API. They are useful when you want evidence that an external consumer can use the package as intended. A practical suite usually combines focused unit tests with a few end-to-end cases. Tests do not prove an implementation correct for every input, but they make intended behavior executable and guard against later changes. Run the narrowest relevant test while editing and the full suite before shipping; both speeds of feedback matter.

Compare `cargo test` and `cargo test --release`: both execute assertions. Integer overflow checks normally differ between the default dev and release profiles, and projects can override that policy. Write explicit checked arithmetic when overflow is part of the API contract, rather than relying on the test profile.
writing.feedback: A test with no assertion only proves the code did not panic.

recall.question: How do unit tests in a `#[cfg(test)]` module differ from integration tests in `tests/` in what they can reach?
recall.answer: Unit tests sit beside the code and, via `use super::*`, can test private helpers. Integration tests compile as separate crates and see only the public API, so they check that an outside consumer can use the package as intended.

recall.question: A test calls `add(u32::MAX, 1)` where `add` returns `a + b`. Why can it behave differently under `cargo test` and `cargo test --release`?
recall.answer: The default dev profile enables integer overflow checks, so the addition panics; the release profile normally disables them, so it wraps to `0`. If overflow is part of the contract, use explicit checked arithmetic rather than relying on the profile.
